# Exercise 6.2 — SHAP, one patient at a time {#sec-shap}


## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Compute SHAP values for a fitted forest and check that they add up to the
  prediction.
- Read a beeswarm plot and a force plot, and say in one sentence what the model
  did for one named patient.
- Say why a SHAP summary and a logistic regression coefficient are not
  comparable until one of them is rescaled.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-importance gave you two rankings, both of them averages over 231 people.
Neither can answer the question a clinician actually asks in front of a
patient: *why this number, for her?* SHAP answers exactly that, and then lets
you average the per-patient answers back up into a global picture. It is the
most useful tool on this day and the easiest to overclaim with, which is why it
sits between the measure that was plainly describing the model (6.1) and the
chapter that says so in R (@sec-dalex).

::: {.callout-note}
## This chapter is Python only
`shap` is a Python library with no equivalent of comparable maturity in R. R
gets its local explanations from DALEX in @sec-dalex, by a different algorithm
(sampling-based Shapley values) that answers the same question. Read this
chapter even if you intend to work in R: the ideas transfer and the plots are
the ones you will be shown by other people.
:::

## The model, again, and its SHAP values

Each chapter is a fresh session, so we refit the forest from @sec-importance —
same data, same split, same control column.

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import shap

# trim the surrounding whitespace when a figure is saved; shap's force plot
# draws outside the axes and is otherwise clipped at the top
matplotlib.rcParams["savefig.bbox"] = "tight"
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

dia = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
y = (dia["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X = dia.drop(columns=["diabetes"]).copy()
X["noise"] = np.random.default_rng(42).normal(size=len(X)).round(2)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=123, stratify=y)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=123).fit(X_train, y_train)
auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, rf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
print("test AUC", round(auc, 3))
```

A SHAP value is one number per patient per variable: how much that variable
moved *this* patient's predicted probability away from the base value, where
the base value is the average prediction over the training rows. The values are
constructed so that they add up exactly:

$$\hat{p}(x_i) = \phi_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{ij}$$

with $\phi_0$ the base value and $\phi_{ij}$ the contribution of variable $j$
to patient $i$. That identity is the whole reason SHAP is worth more than an
importance bar chart: it is an exact decomposition of a specific prediction,
not a summary statistic.

```{python}
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf)
sv = explainer.shap_values(X_test)          # (patients, variables, classes)
phi = sv[:, :, 1]                           # the 'pos' class
base = explainer.expected_value[1]

print("shape", sv.shape)
print("base value", round(base, 3), " training prevalence", round(y_train.mean(), 3))
```

The base value is the training prevalence, as it must be: with no information
about a patient, the forest's best guess is the average.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## How long this takes, and what to do if it is slow
`TreeExplainer` is exact for forests and it explains these 231 test patients in
well under a second. Cost grows with the number of patients, trees and tree
depth, so a larger forest or the full 768 rows will take longer. If it does,
explain a random subsample — `X_test.sample(100, random_state=1)` — and say in
your write-up that you did. A beeswarm of 100 patients looks almost identical
to one of 231; a mean absolute SHAP value computed from 100 is a little
noisier.
:::

## Global view 1 — the bar plot

Averaging $|\phi_{ij}|$ down the patients gives a global importance: how much
this variable moves predictions, in probability units, for a typical patient.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
shap.summary_plot(phi, X_test, plot_type="bar", show=False, plot_size=(7.5, 3.5))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Task 1 — The beeswarm, and the control again

The bar plot throws away everything except the magnitude. The beeswarm keeps
it: one dot per patient per variable, placed at its SHAP value, coloured by how
high that patient's value of the variable was. Draw it, then run the control
check on the mean absolute SHAP values.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

shap.summary_plot(______, X_test, show=False, plot_size=(6.5, 4))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

shap_importance = pd.Series(np.abs(______).mean(axis=0), index=X.columns)
check_noise_control(shap_importance)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

shap.summary_plot(phi, X_test, show=False, plot_size=(6.5, 4))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

shap_importance = pd.Series(np.abs(phi).mean(axis=0), index=X.columns)
print(shap_importance.sort_values(ascending=False).round(4))
check_noise_control(shap_importance)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Both blanks want the same object: the matrix of SHAP values for the positive
class that you built above. `np.abs()` and `.mean(axis=0)` collapse it down the
patients.
:::

Read three things off the beeswarm before you move on.

1. Glucose: the red dots are on the right. High glucose pushes the prediction
   up, consistently, and by up to 0.4 in probability.
2. Pressure and triceps: a vertical smudge at zero. The model barely uses them.
3. `noise`: a smudge too — but a slightly wider one than pressure's, and the
   control check fails again, at around 12% of glucose. SHAP is honest about
   the model, and the model does use the noise column.

## Local view — one patient

Now the thing the averages could not do. Patient 0 of the test set:

```{python}
i = 0
x_i = X_test.iloc[[i]]
print("row", X_test.index[i],
      "| predicted", round(rf.predict_proba(x_i)[0, 1], 3),
      "| actual", "pos" if y_test.iloc[i] == 1 else "neg")
print(x_i.T.rename(columns={X_test.index[i]: "value"}))
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.4
shap.force_plot(base, phi[i], x_i.iloc[0], matplotlib=True, show=False,
                figsize=(16, 3.2))
plt.show()
```

Read the force plot as a tug of war on one number. It starts at the base value
and ends at this patient's prediction; red segments push right, blue segments
push left, and the width of each is its SHAP value. For this patient a glucose
of 167 contributes about +0.31 on its own — more than everything else put
together.

Now the sentence that this chapter exists for. The model gave this patient a
predicted probability of about 0.71. **She does not have diabetes.** The force
plot is still entirely correct: it is a faithful account of how the forest
arrived at 0.71. It is not an account of her physiology, and if you read it
aloud as "her high glucose is driving her diabetes risk" you have changed the
subject without noticing.

## Task 2 — Check the arithmetic

The additivity identity above is a claim you can test. Pick any patient, add
the base value to their SHAP values, and compare with the model's prediction.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

j = 17                                   # any row of the test set
reconstructed = ______ + phi[j].sum()
predicted     = rf.predict_proba(X_test.iloc[[j]])[0, 1]
print(round(reconstructed, 6), round(predicted, 6))
check_metric_range(abs(reconstructed - ______), 0, 1e-6, "reconstruction error")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

j = 17
reconstructed = base + phi[j].sum()
predicted     = rf.predict_proba(X_test.iloc[[j]])[0, 1]
print(round(reconstructed, 6), round(predicted, 6))
check_metric_range(abs(reconstructed - predicted), 0, 1e-6, "reconstruction error")
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The identity has three parts: the base value, the sum of this patient's
contributions, and the prediction. Two of them are already on the line.
:::

The error is of the order of $10^{-16}$. TreeExplainer is not approximating
here — for a tree ensemble it computes the Shapley values exactly.

## A fairer comparison — logistic regression coefficients

The usual next slide puts SHAP next to the coefficients of a logistic
regression and invites you to compare the two rankings. Done naively that
comparison is meaningless, and it is worth seeing why.

```{python}
lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, solver="liblinear",
                        random_state=123).fit(X_train, y_train)
print("logistic regression test AUC", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, lr.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]), 3))

coef = pd.Series(lr.coef_[0], index=X.columns)
print("\nraw coefficients, log-odds per unit:")
print(coef.round(3))
```

The largest coefficient by a factor of five belongs to `pedigree`. That is an
artefact of the units: `pedigree` runs from about 0.08 to 2.4, while `glucose`
runs to 199, so a coefficient "per unit" means something a hundred times
smaller for glucose. Multiply each coefficient by the training standard
deviation of its variable and you have the change in log-odds per standard
deviation, which is comparable across variables.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
coef_sd = (coef * X_train.std()).sort_values()
print(coef_sd.round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
coef_sd.plot(kind="barh", ax=ax, color="mediumseagreen")
ax.axvline(0, color="grey", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("change in log-odds per 1 SD")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

On that scale glucose is the largest by a wide margin and `pedigree` has
dropped to fourth. The ranking reversed because of a unit conversion, not
because of anything in the data.

Two further things are worth noticing. The logistic regression's test AUC is
about the same as the forest's: the black box bought you nothing here, which is
worth remembering before you spend a day explaining it. And `pressure` gets a
substantial *negative* standardised coefficient while the forest gives it
almost no SHAP at all — two models of the same data disagreeing about a
variable, which is a fact about the models.

## Task 3 — Put the four measures side by side

Build one table with a column per method, each scaled to its own maximum so the
columns are on a common footing, and read off where the control sits in each.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

perm = pd.Series(permutation_importance(
    rf, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=20, random_state=123,
    scoring="roc_auc").importances_mean, index=X.columns)

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "impurity":    pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns),
    "permutation": perm,
    "mean |SHAP|": pd.Series(np.abs(phi).mean(axis=0), index=X.columns),
    "|coef| per SD": ______,
})
comparison = comparison / comparison.______()
print(comparison.round(2).sort_values("mean |SHAP|", ascending=False))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

perm = pd.Series(permutation_importance(
    rf, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=20, random_state=123,
    scoring="roc_auc").importances_mean, index=X.columns)

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "impurity":    pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns),
    "permutation": perm,
    "mean |SHAP|": pd.Series(np.abs(phi).mean(axis=0), index=X.columns),
    "|coef| per SD": (coef * X_train.std()).abs(),
})
comparison = comparison / comparison.max()
print(comparison.round(2).sort_values("mean |SHAP|", ascending=False))
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The fourth column is the standardised coefficients you just computed, without
their signs — importance measures have no direction, so take the absolute
value. Scaling a data frame by its column maxima is one method call.
:::

Every column agrees that glucose is first. Below that they disagree about
almost everything, and the `noise` row is between 0 and 0.37 depending on which
method you happened to run.

## The result that should bother you

An explanation does not know whether the model is any good. Here is the same
forest fitted to the same predictors with the outcome column shuffled, so that
there is no relationship left to learn.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
y_shuffled = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(y_train.values)
rf_null = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=123).fit(X_train, y_shuffled)
print("test AUC of the shuffled-label forest:",
      round(roc_auc_score(y_test, rf_null.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]), 3))

phi_null = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_null).shap_values(X_test)[:, :, 1]
shap.summary_plot(phi_null, X_test, show=False, plot_size=(6.5, 4))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The AUC is about 0.47 — worse than a coin toss. The beeswarm is still a
beeswarm: variables are ranked, dots are coloured, one predictor leads the
others by a clear margin. The contributions are about a third the size of the
real model's, which you would only notice by looking at the axis, and `shap`
will not tell you.

1. SHAP explains the function the model computes. It has no access to the
   outcome, so it cannot know the function is worthless.
2. Therefore a SHAP plot is never evidence that a model works. The evidence
   that a model works is a held-out score against a baseline, and it has to
   come first.
3. And the ordering in a SHAP plot of a model that does not work is just the
   ordering of its overfitting.

## Reflection

1. A colleague shows you a beeswarm plot in a slide deck. Write down the two
   questions you would ask before reading anything off it.
2. The force plot for patient 0 was a correct explanation of a prediction that
   was wrong about the patient. Explain, in one sentence each, what the plot
   does and does not license you to say.
3. SHAP values for this model are in probability units and sum to the
   prediction. What would be lost if they were reported on the log-odds scale
   instead, and what would be gained?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) "What is the held-out score, and against what baseline?" and
"what is on the x-axis, and how wide is it?" — the shuffled-label figure above
fails both. (2) It licenses: *the forest's output for this row was 0.71, and of
the 0.35 above the base rate, about 0.31 came from the glucose value of 167.*
It does not license any statement about her risk, her physiology, or what would
happen if her glucose fell. The last one needs a causal model, not an
attribution. (3) Log-odds are additive in the way logistic regression is
additive, so contributions are comparable across patients with very different
baseline risks; probability units are directly interpretable to a clinician but
compress near 0 and 1, so the same physiological change produces a smaller
$\phi$ for an already-low-risk patient.

**Expected values.** Base value equals the training prevalence, 0.36–0.37. Mean
|SHAP|: glucose 0.15–0.16, everything else under 0.06, `noise` about 0.02 and
around 12% of glucose. Patient 0 is predicted 0.70–0.72 and is a true negative;
glucose contributes about +0.31. Reconstruction error of order 1e-16. Logistic
regression AUC 0.75–0.77, i.e. indistinguishable from the forest. Shuffled-label
forest AUC 0.44–0.52.

**Common failures.** (1) Indexing `shap_values` as `sv[1]` — in `shap` 0.45 and
later the array is (patients, variables, classes), and older tutorials assume a
list of two arrays. If a student's plot looks mirrored, this is why. (2)
Forgetting `show=False`, so the figure is drawn twice or not at all. (3)
Reading the force plot as a causal claim about the patient; this is the one to
stop the room for. (4) Comparing raw coefficients with SHAP values and
concluding something about `pedigree`.

**Timing.** Task 3 is the one to cut. The shuffled-label example at the end is
not optional — it is the payload of the whole day.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Two patients with the same prediction
Find two test patients whose predicted probabilities agree to within 0.01 and
plot a force plot for each. If the explanations differ, what does that tell you
about the model that the prediction alone did not?
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Explain the logistic regression instead
`shap.LinearExplainer` gives SHAP values for the logistic regression. Compute
them and compare with the standardised coefficients. They should agree almost
exactly, and the reason they do tells you what SHAP adds for a forest and does
not add for a linear model.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that for this forest, this patient's prediction of 0.71 decomposes
exactly into a base rate of 0.37 plus a set of contributions dominated by
glucose; and that the same decomposition, done on a model that cannot predict
anything, looks much the same.

**Cannot:** that glucose caused anything, that lowering it would lower the
prediction for a future patient, or that the forest has found something about
diabetes. The first of those needs a causal question asked properly; the others
need an experiment. @sec-dalex asks the same questions in R, and adds the one
plot that at least *looks* like an intervention — and shows why it is not one.
